newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore shipyards face rough time next year.
newsitem.headline: Singapore shipyards face rough time next year.

text.p: Singapore's long-suffering shipyards will continue to face rough seas in 1997, with the outlook for ship repair remaining dismal, marine analysts said.
"The outlook for the yards in 1997 is still rough," said Neil Payne, head of research at ING Barings.
"I think the recovery has been delayed because the results from ship repairs are still poor. There has been no recovery in ship repairs," Payne said.
Singapore has four major yards -- Keppel Shipyard, Sembawang Corp, Jurong Shipyard and Hitachi Zosen
Some analysts estimated the combined operating profits of the big four yards in 1996 would erode by about 45 percent from 1995 to about Singapore $47.8 million (US$34.1 million).
Under a best case scenario, they added, the aggregate profit growth was unlikely to exceed 16 percent in 1997/98.
In the 1991/92 boom period, profits for the industry soared 30-40 percent.
Last December, Singapore's Economic Development board (EDB) predicted growth in the marine industry in 1996 would be powered by shipbuilding and conversion activities.
Analysts said the EDB might have been too bullish.
"Shipbuilding has been facing increasing competition from low cost builders, especially in China," Payne said. "There just doesn't seem to have that many conversions in 1996."
"The turnover for ship repair and conversions is down hard and margins have been squeezed. So you have a double-whammy, hitting the bottom-line more," an analyst from a European institution said.

While ship repair volume had been buoyed by firmer freight rates, analysts said these gains could be undermined by higher capacities, competition from the Middle East and China as well as surplus shipbuilding capacities.

"Surplus dock capacity is a worry. The yards have not managed to stabilise falling ship repair prices and margins amid relentless competition from the Middle East rivals," the analyst with the European institution said.

Two new docks by Keppel Shipyard and Jurong Shipyard opened in the second half of this year are expected to exacerbate the surplus repair capacity lifting capacity by 31 percent to three million dead weight tonnes (dwt).
A potential cut in shipbuilding prices by South Korea in order to fill their yards was also a concern, analysts said.
But analysts said shipbuilding was not a sunset industry in Singapore.

"To call it a sunset industry will not be totally true. We have a locational advantage, sophisticated infrastructure. Ship repairs need spare parts and supporting industry to give a quick turnaround," the analyst from the European institution said.
Analysts said the industry was ripe for rationalisation. The proposed merger between Sembawang and Jurong was seen as a move in this direction.
In the proposed merger, Sembawang would merge its ship repair and marine engineering businesses with Jurong Shipyard.
Analysts said Singapore would still face surplus dock capacity and a margin squeeze unless the Sembawang dry docks were closed.

Sembawang is expected to redevelop its 8.8 million sq ft (820,000 sq m) yard, with a total dock capacity of 740,000 dwt, into a residential project. The earliest the yard would make way for property development is in the second half of 1998.
"If not, these docks will still have to be filled. That still means competition," said a DBS Investment analyst.
Until the rationalisation is complete, analysts said they continued to underweight the sector.
